[[Incumbent]] [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Phil Bredesen]] was re-elected to a second term with 68.6% of the vote, defeating his [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] challenger, [[Jim Bryson (politician)|Jim Bryson]]. Improving on his performance from [[2002 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2002]], Bredesen also carried every county in the state.{{Cite web |title=2006 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Tennessee |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2006&fips=47&off=5&elect=0&f=0 |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this was the last time a Democrat won a majority of counties in the state, the last time a Democrat won any statewide race in Tennessee, and the most recent statewide election in Tennessee in which 83 of the state's 95 counties voted Democratic. Only [[Davidson County, Tennessee|Davidson]], [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Hamilton]], [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Haywood]], [[Hardeman County, Tennessee|Hardeman]], [[Houston County, Tennessee|Houston]], [[Jackson County, Tennessee|Jackson]], [[Knox County, Tennessee|Knox,]] [[Lake County, Tennessee|Lake]], [[Madison County, Tennessee|Madison,]] [[Montgomery County, Tennessee|Montgomery]], [[Rutherford County, Tennessee|Rutherford]], and [[Shelby County, Tennessee|Shelby]] counties have voted for a Democratic candidate in a presidential, senatorial, or gubernatorial race since 2006. Eight years after this, Republican governor [[Bill Haslam]] would win every county in the state when he won [[2014 Tennessee gubernatorial election|re-election]]. == Background == [[Phil Bredesen]] became governor amid a fiscal crisis, with a predicted state budget shortfall of $800 million. Much of the shortfall was due to TennCare, which was $650 million over budget.{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Gov. Phil Bredesen (D) |url=http://www.nationaljournal.com/almanac/2010/person/phil-bredesen-tn/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130216123308/http://www.nationaljournal.com/almanac/2010/person/phil-bredesen-tn/ |archive-date=2013-02-16 |work=National Journal Magazine}} Sundquist had hoped to remedy the budget shortfall by implementing an income tax, but this proved wildly unpopular and was never enacted.{{cite web |author=Roger Abramson |date=2011-01-06 |title=Phil Bredesen Made a Successful Governor for One Mind-blowing Reason: He Did Just What He Said |url=http://www.nashvillescene.com/nashville/phil-bredesen-made-a-successful-governor-for-one-mind-blowing-reason-he-did-just-what-he-said/Content?oid=2138062 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221656/http://www.nashvillescene.com/nashville/phil-bredesen-made-a-successful-governor-for-one-mind-blowing-reason-he-did-just-what-he-said/Content?oid=2138062 |archive-date=March 3, 2016 |access-date=January 14, 2013 |work=The Nashville Scene}} Bredesen argued that services would have to be cut, saying, "you can't have Massachusetts services and Tennessee taxes." In 2003, he signed a 9% across-the-board spending cut. In 2004, he enacted a series of changes to TennCare, essentially removing 191,000 [[Medicaid]]-eligible patients and reducing benefits. By 2006, these changes had reduced the program's cost by more than $500 million. Bredesen used some of the savings to establish a "safety net" for health clinics affected by the cuts.
